Ozempic side effect Depression 
Reader’s Discretion is Advised: 

I was taking ozempic for good amount of time and when I reached at highest doze my emotions changed. I did lost alot of weight too. But my folks and siblings noticed how I was behaving in general. I became more irritable, angry , and started to get more depressed.

I initially thought it maybe because of some other factor in my life. Or maybe my vitamin D was low. And kept taking ozempic. To the point I was thinking of self harm. My mental health deteriorated very very much. I joined some online group how to handle such thoughts and emotions. But they were not of much help. I never had these kinds of thoughts in my life. I was googling stuff that I clearly should not, to harm myself. I did cut off from everyone; my parents, friends and siblings. Long story short, my parents who were trying to help me and asked to stop taking ozempic all together. 

I cancelled ozempic 2 months ago and slowly my depressive thoughts are gone. I have focused to drop weight the old fashioned way. I am just sharing to those who are having same experience and they should keep an eye on their mental health. Peace ☮️ be upon you all! And take care!

Misinformation!
Why is there so much negative and bad information out there about Ozempic? 

First off, it’s a drug used to treat a medical condition so I’m not going to listen to someone without a medical degree.

Some people are haters, and/or jealous, and some people just are fear mongering or don’t really realize how awesome this drug is for some people. 

Every single drug out there has the ability to have negative side effects. So why is it with this drug that people feel the need to warn you to be careful, tell you how it’s going to affect your body, or just say dumb shit in general. 

I literally had a friend say to me today that the Covid vaccine is in Ozempic. This is by far the stupidest thing I’ve ever heard and now it’s coming from the stupidest person I know. I wonder if she’s saying that because she knows I didn’t react well to the Covid vaccine . I know she’s not my greatest fan or supporter. I no longer talk to her about it, but she keeps bringing it up. Personally, I’m offended that she thinks I’m that stupid that I would listen to her misinformation.

Others just want to focus on the  potential bad side effects and continuously remind you of all the negative things that can happen. 

Just a rent, but as time goes on, Ozempic is literally being given credit for reducing compulsive and addictive behaviors, lowering chances for dementia, heart, disease, stroke, not to mention diabetes and other weight related conditions. 

This has been such a good drug for me. I even have a friend who is a diabetic who is a very well meaning person who’s telling me you can manage this with a diet and a pill. I’m assuming she’s meeting metformin which is really a drug with potential side effects 

Long ran short, but I’m just wondering, why are there so many people that are haters of this drug ?

Hi y’all!

I gained a lot of weight through the course of my two pregnancies in the past 4 years and just needed some help getting to a better bmi.

Will make this post short but happy to answer questions in comments! Basically had long/heavy and irregular periods + cystic acne growing up. Around the age of 20 I got put on Yaz and it cleared up the acne and made my periods virtually go away. I started ozempic about 6 weeks ago and went up to .5mg recently. For over a week now I have been spotting, nonstop. My acne has flared up, even on my back, having mild period cramps, and my breasts are intermittently tender. I’m so confused! I know it’s the ozempic as nothing else has changed and I haven’t had any hormonal type side effects like this in over 7 years since being on Yaz. I’ve seen people say it may be the weight loss causing it but I’ve only lost like 2-3lbs lol and I’ve never had this happen before when losing way more weight. 

I’m a little worried. I can’t tell if ozempic is bringing to light a hormonal issue I’ve always had that was masked by the pill or if it’s just overall reducing the efficacy of the pill? I’m nervous to take a medication when no studies have even shown this as a side effect despite me absolutely positive it IS a side effect. Has anyone else had this happen?

Persistent nausea and gastroparesis
I started taking Ozempic for Type II Diabetes that has never been able to be controlled in 22 years. It seems to be my last ditch effort, and it did. However, the nausea began almost immediately. Always in the morning and always vomiting liquid that eventually would become bile. I would vomit after I would eat and still, only liquid ever came up. I developed chronic gastroparesis and it comes and goes. I started Tresiba insulin 2 months in to the Ozempic. I am also insulin resistant. 

I stopped Ozempic 4 months after starting because I could no longer live with the nausea. I had lost only 8 pounds. Blood sugar went up drastically. I was nauseous every day, always still vomiting liquid. I lost 30 pounds in 3 months. While the weight loss was awesome, it came off very quickly as I could not  eat or get proper nutrition. I started daily Zofran. Sublingual worked almost immediately but the pill form did not. I took that every morning and it would take a few hours. 

All of my weight came back at that point as I had an appetite after almost a year. Thus, my blood sugar raised. I was taken off of Metformin after 22 years and told to only use the Tresiba. My sugar is almost out of control again. I still have nausea and gastroparesis comes and goes. I am on a waitlist to get into a gastroenterologist before March...at a huge hospital system. My appetite continues to be out of control and I am almost never sated. No food doesn't make me sick at this point. I used to be able to eat bland foods: only pretzels, saltines, and jello. 

I have to lose the weight again, but nothing is working, the nausea is every morning and vomiting is sparse. I only drink water and sometimes ginger ale. I've always had GI issues, two colonoscopies, and misdiagnosed with Crohn's. I had a CT done several months ago and nothing was found. I have many food sensitivities, lactose intolerant, etc.

I am at my breaking point and have no idea what I need to do or where to go. Has anyone experienced similar?

Ozempic for non obese patients
Hello. I 30F, have PCOS and insulin resistance. I was always skinny and pretty healthy, until COVID hit and I ate my way to gain 30lb in 12 months. 
After that all the symptoms of the PCOS I didn’t know I had started showing up, and I have been struggling with my weight for all these 3 years. 

In 2020, besides gaining weight I developed anxiety and depression, so no need to say it was a tough time. I’ve been craving sugar like an animal and it’s just being a disaster for my self-esteem. I hate what I look like, I hate feeling like a loser because I can’t do anything about it , I hate feeling so weak. 

Last month I went to the doctor and my cholesterol is very high, so the doctor prescribed me Ozempic to kick start my weight loss. I only have to lose a total of 25lb ~ ; so I’m not obese. However; my BMI is over 30 so it’s a health concern now. Ozempic will be to jump start my weight loss. 

Did anyone here have results only on 0.25? Do I really have to increase it to 0.5? I am afraid of the side effects of 0.5 

Did anyone here take Ozempic but “only” had to lose up to 30lb? Please share some positive stories. Everything I read is making me fear starting Ozempic SO BAD

How I am dealing with the shortage
Original post 2.5 months ago

https://www.reddit.com/r/Ozempic/s/OuKX6jQdS1

Hey there again! I loved connecting with so many others who were not seeing results right away! I felt so inspired by your messages. 

Over the last 2.5  months since my last post, I started adjusting when I was taking my shot. Food noise was coming back sooner and sooner, and I was up to 2.3mg/week (1mg every 3rd day). It was getting pricey and I was starting to worry that i’d plateau at the max dose before reaching my  Ideal weight. I started in March at 211, and at the point I was taking 2.3 I was around 171-173 (i use a shapa scale so I don’t know the exact number). 

3 weeks ago I called my pharmacy for my refill (on injection day), and was told the stock was gone. I went on the waitlist and have been 3rd on the list since then with no movement. 

The pharmacist (bless her) said there was an oral option that I should talk to my doctor about, but it was not in their scope to discuss off label use with me.

My doc squeezed me in 4 days after my missed injection. The stress normally would have triggered a binge and I definitely had the appetite but I channeled my energy into remembering how far i’ve come. 

My doc and I decided to try Rybelsus. I’m not diabetic and my doctor was not very familiar with the medication. From what I had researched, 14mg a day was equivalent to 1mg/week injection, I advocated to go with the full dose and she supported me. 

Rybelsus works best on an empty stomach, and fasting after for at least 30 min. What I have been doing is getting up 1 hour before I normally would, taking the Rybelsus and then going back to sleep. I find it’s been very effective, instead of the waves of nausea on injection day and then food noise the day before, a daily pill has been a great baseline feeling for me, I hope it lasts and I would be fine to stay on this if Ozempic is out of stock longterm. 

Not medical advice, but just wanted to share my experience with a substitute medication. Some say it is not as effective but I feel a stronger response to this medication than 2.3/week of injection. I weighed in at 168 today so I am back to 1-2lbs a week of weight loss :)

Hair loss - did it stop even after *staying* on Ozempic?
I have seen a lot of posts with people saying the hair loss became so sever that they went off Ozempic. Some say it came back after and others say it still did not come back. 

I know hair loss can happen with rapid weight loss - but *many* people say it happened even when they weren’t losing much. I myself have lost weight this rapidly before (fasting, life events) and never had hair loss. This time, after 3 months on Oz I have a LOT of hair loss. I need to empty my hairbrush every other day.

I am eating protein, eating enough, etc. I am inclined to believe some is from the weight loss, and some/more is from Oz itself - as many others have speculated. 

*I do not need more info on hair loss from rapid weight loss/tele effluvium.*

My question is - has anyone had bad hair loss, but stayed on ozempic anyway, and had it slow down or stop? How many months after the shedding began did it stop? Did you take Nutrafol, red light therapy, Rogaine (topical or pill), etc?

If my shedding doesn’t stop, I will become bald and that would devastate me. Thank you!

Small changes, big impact!
I was diagnosed with PCOS and pre-diabetes a few months ago. My cholesterol is at 240, my weight is 160lbs/ 73kg, height is 5’3”. I was ruled out for hypothyroidism, but have two, slightly big cervical lymph nodes that my doctors are monitoring, was told I have a hormonal imbalance and insulin resistance. I was never able to shed off even a bit of weight through workouts and diets.

I was given metformin first, then prescribed Ozempic after 50 tablets of metformin. Here’s what happened during my first week on Ozempic:

* Started, first week: September 3, 2023, Sunday at 11:30 pm
- Dosage: 0.25mg, no pain, didn’t feel anything
- Day 1, Monday: A bit of nausea in the morning, regular bathroom visits and nausea at night
- Day 2, Tuesday: No appetite in the morning, ate late lunch, upset stomach but nothing too bad, mild nausea in the late afternoon but went away after I had a pack of crackers for dinner. No usual late-night cravings. Stomach cramps before bed. (Sleeping sideways with one leg up, in a “4” position, eased some of the cramping)
- Day 3, Wednesday: diarrhea in the morning, played 18 holes of golf, and felt nauseous on the last 4 holes. Felt nauseous while walking around in the afternoon and had to take an anti-nausea pill as I felt like my body was about to pass out on me. Diarrhea after dinner. No usual late-night cravings. Stomach cramps before bed.
- Day 4, Thursday: No diarrhea, had an appetite for lunch and dinner although it was only half a serving than my usual. No usual late-night cravings.
- Day 5, Friday: played 18 holes of golf, had quite a lot of energy (I usually get tired towards the end, but I was feeling great!) had a late lunch and late dinner- my appetite was good, and ate half my usual serving and felt fully satisfied. No usual late-night cravings.
- Day 6, Saturday: had an appetite for lunch, had matcha in the afternoon, and had a very small appetite for dinner
- Day 7, Sunday: had a late lunch and a bit of dinner. No symptoms to note
- Weigh in: -3 lbs

While on Ozempic, I noticed I did not have any late-night cravings and my mindset seemed to shift from eating because I was bored or just because there was food in my fridge to eating when I felt hungry and being mindful of what I eat. In my household, there are usually 3-4 plates of food for meals. I would usually go for the fried, unhealthy plates, but now, I prefer the healthy plates (e.g.: vegetables, soup, fish)

I wouldn’t overfill my plate, but rather, get enough (palm-sized servings) at a time. I find on average, a palm-sized serving is enough for me and I’d have crackers throughout the day until my next meal. Most of the time, I’d have soup for dinner as the crackers made me full. One big thing I noticed was staying full longer! 

For more context:
- “nausea”/ “nauseous: I feel gross, but not enough to throw up
- “Appetite”: I feel as though I can have more than a “palm-sized” serving
- Snacks are usually a pack of crackers or a sandwich split into 6 bite-sized pieces and eaten throughout the day
- My usual late-night cravings would be full-sized meals or unhealthy and quick ready-made meals
- Anti-nausea meds: bonamine chewable tablet
- “stomach cramps”: felt like day 2 of period cramps
- Doctors I see regularly: endocrinologist, OBGYN, nutritionist, and psychologist.

The biggest differences:
- feeling full for much longer
- Choosing the healthier option
- having more energy throughout the day
- sleeping better
- not in a crap mood all the time
- Seeing that I lost 3lbs after being at 160lbs for a while

I don’t know if this would help anyone, but for those of you who have any questions, my inbox is always open and for those who are interested, I may just keep updating on this post. Just remember that everyone has a different reaction to medicine and I wish everyone on this Ozempic journey the best of luck!!

AMA from Weight Loss Professional
**Hello All!**

I’ve been reading posts in this group for a while, and I wanted to share some general information that might be helpful. First, let me introduce myself. I’m a Physician Assistant (PA) who owns and operates a medical weight loss clinic in Maryland. My background is in acute care (working in the Emergency Room and Urgent Care), where I saw how weight often played a big role in many health problems. That’s why I designed my practice to conveniently serve people in Maryland and nearby areas. I’m not claiming to be the ultimate expert, but after reading some of your posts, I felt the need to share some advice. This is kind of like an AMA (Ask Me Anything), except you don’t have to ask first. Please see my disclaimer at the bottom.

**TL;DR:** Everyone’s healthcare should be personalized to fit their needs and goals. I believe these medications offer one of the best ways to prevent disease, rather than just treating symptoms after they appear. While there are many benefits (weight loss, heart protection, nerve protection, kidney protection, prevention of Type 2 diabetes, reduced inflammation, and joint pain relief), there are also some side effects (nausea, stomach cramps, constipation, diarrhea, gallbladder issues, and pancreatitis). Medicine is all about balancing risks and benefits, and these medications offer many advantages.

First and foremost, please understand that injectable GLP-1 medications are not miracle cures. They won’t work overnight, and they won’t solve all your problems. While I often mention Semaglutide, the advice I give here also applies to Tirzepatide (and Retatrutide, though be cautious with this peptide at it is only approved for research).

**Popular Questions:**

**1) What do all of these abbreviations mean?** 

• **GLP-1 (Glucagon-like peptide 1):** A hormone that helps regulate blood sugar by increasing insulin secretion, slowing digestion, and promoting fullness. 

https://preview.redd.it/sl5ftwj6pgnd1.png?width=1548&format=png&auto=webp&s=85501f6aeb09161c41495611315b60ae6fa9b0b2

• **GIP (Glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide):** A hormone that stimulates insulin release, especially after consuming carbs. 

https://preview.redd.it/4atapkm5qgnd1.png?width=383&format=png&auto=webp&s=f11b1fc4c5a4e7b341211575073a4816e8e295db

• **GA (Glucagon receptor agonist):** A drug that activates glucagon receptors, helping raise blood sugar and reduce appetite. 

• **MEN (Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia):** A group of hereditary disorders that can cause tumors in the endocrine glands. 

• **MTC (Medullary Thyroid Carcinoma):** A type of thyroid cancer that may be linked to genetic conditions like MEN 2.

**2) How do these medications work?** 

• **Semaglutide:** Mimics GLP-1, controlling blood sugar by boosting insulin, slowing stomach emptying, and reducing appetite. 

• **Tirzepatide:** Targets both GLP-1 and GIP receptors, offering enhanced blood sugar control and greater weight loss compared to GLP-1 medications alone. 

• **Retatrutide:** A newer medication in trials that targets GLP-1, GIP, and GA receptors to help with blood sugar control and appetite reduction, offering broader benefits.

**3) Where should I get my medication?** Get your medication from a reliable, cost-effective source. Here’s my order of preference: 

• **Primary Care Provider (through insurance):** Usually the cheapest if covered; however, difficult to get from pharmacy due to shortages. 

• **Local Weight Loss Clinic/MedSpa:** Provides more personalized care. My patients can text me directly with questions. 

• **Nationwide Weight Loss Clinic:** These can offer the best pricing, but the service quality can be questionable. I've had patients switch to my clinic from nationwide companies and see better results. Some nationwide clinics may offer compounded medications that might be diluted or not come from a US regulated pharmacy (ie you are getting reconstituted research product).  No reputable pharmacy is making compound for $99/mo and still making profit.  If the nationwide company is unable to send you the certificate of analysis, RUN.  To be safe, the compounding pharmacy should be FDA and board of pharmacy regulated and they are getting medication from an FDA approved manufacture.

**4) I just started, why haven’t I seen results?** Results take time. Be patient with yourself. You didn’t gain weight in one month, and you won’t lose it all in one month. Consistency is key to long-term success.

**5) What diet plan should I follow?** There’s no one-size-fits-all answer. I generally recommend: 

• **High protein** to support muscle and satiety. 

• **High water intake** for hydration and appetite control. 

• **High fiber** for digestion and fullness. 

• **Lower carbs and fats** to manage blood sugar and calories. 

• **Avoid** fasting or eating only one meal a day, as it can slow digestion.

**6) Why do others talk negatively about people taking weight loss medications?** Unfortunately, there is a lot of stigma around using these medications. As a healthcare provider, I find this completely inappropriate. Just like I wouldn’t think twice about giving antibiotics to someone with a life-threatening infection, I don’t see why anyone should think negatively about someone trying to lose weight with medication. A doctor on TikTok compared these medications to penicillin in terms of their impact on healthcare, and I have to agree. They offer a real chance to promote health beyond just telling someone to diet and exercise.

As for your friends and family, remember that it’s none of their business. You’re not "taking this from diabetics" or doing anything wrong. High BMI is a serious health issue, leading to many complications, just like any other condition. Please, don’t feel ashamed. It’s nobody else’s business, but if you choose to share, be proud. You’ve taken the first step in taking control of your health and not falling prey to the availability of unhealthy foods in society.

**7) How are people “overdosing” on these medications?** Compounded medications often come in a vial, so you have to measure and inject the right amount yourself. This can lead to mistakes, like giving yourself 25 units when you see “2.5 mg/mL” on the bottle. Be very careful when injecting. If you have any questions, contact your provider—they’re there to help. This is new for a lot of people, so it’s okay if you’re unsure at first. The good news is that even if you accidentally inject a full syringe (100 units), it’s usually not an overdose. This would likely be the highest dose, and while you might feel really bad for about 4-5 days, it should pass. If you’re concerned, don’t hesitate to go to the ER.

**8) How do I get over side effects?** Talk to your provider. Here are some common side effects and tips to manage them: 

• **Nausea:** Try Zofran, ginger, vitamin B6, or Dramamine. 

• **Diarrhea/Constipation:** Increase fiber intake. 

• **Burping:** Take an antacid. 

• **Hair loss:** Supplement Vitamin D3 (1500 IU) with K2. 

• **"Ozempic Face" (loss of facial fat and muscle mass):** Do strength training and increase protein. 

• **Dizziness:** Hydrate with electrolytes. 

• **Fatigue:** At least 7 hours of sleep, consume at least 0.5g of protein per pound of body weight, take a multivitamin.

• **Sweet Cravings:** Typically due to fluctuations of your glucose levels while your body is getting used to medications; will get better with time.

**9) I have stalled on my medication, what do I do now?**  Usually, the solution is simple—give it time. Make sure you’re getting the right amount of protein, staying hydrated, and rotating your injection sites (abdomen, thigh, arm).

**10) Do I have to take this forever?**  Probably, but not always. Let me explain: You’re using this medication to help correct certain processes in your body. It’s not necessarily that you have a biological defect, but these medications aid in getting your body on the right track for processes that might not be strong enough on their own.

If you stop suddenly, you’re likely to regain the weight. I recommend my patients stay on the medication for 3-5 years to maintain a steady state. This is something that's hard to fully understand until you've gone through it yourself. Imagine walking into the break room and seeing your coworker’s famous chocolate chip cookies. You’re trying to stick to your diet, so you pass on the cookies. But then, for the next four hours, you can’t stop thinking about them. You’re almost salivating, and your stomach is growling. By the time lunch rolls around, you give in and eat three cookies, totaling 500 calories and 20 grams of carbs, leaving you feeling like a failure. This might lead you to declare the whole day a “cheat day,” derailing your dietary goals for the week.

Patients who use these medications often find that they can control or completely avoid these situations because the "food noise" is silenced. They no longer feel the overwhelming urge to give in to cravings, which helps them stay on track with their goals.

I have a family doctor as mentioned earlier, but since we're headed toward a way to treat the symptoms, I thought I'd try asking on Reddit to see if anyone could help finding the cause(s) of my problems.

Hello everyone, I'm at a bit of a bad place right now and I've been looking for information / support / acknowledgement that this exists from strangers. I don't really know what good it will do me, but I hope by getting myself out there it can help my mental health a bit.

Bit of a back story. I'm 36 now and I've had anxiety all my life. It started when I was 9 and I chocked on a tortilla from taco johns. From there I remember infrequent times where I was hungry I would shake uncontrollably. I didnt always have the best food options growing up but I learned to live with it. As an adult I would have panic attacks if I went to long without eating. The symptoms were essentially copy and pasted what hypoglycemia would look like. However my blood sugar during these times was fine.

I've been on lexapro for about a decade now and my anxiety was under control with the trigger listed above as the only thing I had to actively manage. With needing to eat to avoid panic attacks, you can imagine it was hard to control my weight.

Cue last september, I had a burning sensation when taking a pee. Turns out I was passing sugar in my urine. It's type 2 diabetes time! I immediately took control the best I could with dietary changes. I lost about 25 lbs in a few months on my own adding victoza about 6 weeks after my diagnosis. I had wanted ozempic as many of my friends were on it. I was also scared of metformin because of its rare interaction with alcohol. 

Late january we had a shortage of victoza here. At the same time I conveniently got a letter in the mail that my insurance would now cover ozempic. I had been stable and doing quite well. My weight had plateaued but my blood sugar was under control. Now it's time to restart the process but hopefully lose more weight! Around 2/23 I started my first dose of ozempic. 

April 10th was my first episode. officially I was diagnosed with fainting. I was sleeping in bed and I woke up and something felt off. I was overwhelmed with panic and rushed out and immediately fainted. I went to the ER and after a battery of tests nothing was found to be wrong with me. 

May 1st it happened again. This time my primary started my on buspar to help with the anxiety. I had high hopes that this was just my anxiety and this would fix it. It lasted all of 2 weeks.

May 15th was just a few days ago now. I've had some normal and some not so normal days between my last 2 dr visits but something broke for me this morning. I was looking at something and had a feeling of nostalgia and it triggered a panic attack. I was stuck in that moment and everything I did to look forwards felt hopeless. I woke my wife and tried to have her help calm me down. After talking to her I was feeling numb and felt like doing things to feel again. I wanted to hit the walls, bite myself, or anything to feel real. Thats when I decided to go in again, these thoughts were not my own. 

In the ER they have me ativan which calmed me down. I made an appointment with my primary and saw her that afternoon. We agreed to stop the buspar and the ozempic as well. We feel as if the ozempic nausea is triggering my anxiety and the buspar seems to have exasperated it rather than help. It's been 8 days since my last shot of ozempic. I'm taking hydroxyzine for the anxiety episodes. It helps but makes me sleepy. Last night I had nightmares and when I woke up i couldnt stay awake long enough to get away from them due to the sedative effect. I think I'll try and ride out the day without them. 

For now I'm trying to take it a minute at a time, an hour at a time, a day at a time. Each time I have a slight bit of nausea its sugar coated with anxiety. We are hoping that once the ozempic leaves my body ill return to how I was before and able to manage my anxiety.

I have a degree in epidemiology (MPH) and it is legitimate to report hazard ratios as percentages. You did have a good explaination of how odds ratios/hazard ratios work, basically they are comparing the odds of the occurrence (during a specific length of time) in one group to another group. So if there is 1/100 in a control group and and 2/100 in the GLP 1 group, that would be an hazard ratio of 2.0. Another way to report an hazard ratio is to say there is a 100% increase in incidence when taking a GLP1. It definitely sounds confusing when we talk about 100%, but when the hazard ratio is 1.20, for example, we call that a 20% increase. 

Another important factor when reporting data is to always take things in context of their 95% confidence interval. The confidence interval tells us the predicted outcome for 95% of situations. Here is an excerpt from the study:

>Notably, the Ozempic group showed an HR of 1.72 (95% CI 1.67–1.76)

You can interpret this to mean they are 95% confident that Ozempic increased any psychiatric diseass by 67% to 76%. 

I do agree that misunderstanding about interpreting statistics can be confusing. For example, I have an 87% lifetime risk of breast cancer due to BRCA1. However I once spoke with a doctor who believed that I had an 87% increased risk of breast cancer (Odds Ratio 1.87). However my risk is actually 87% lifetime compared to 12% lifetime in the general population, which means it is an odds ratio of 7.25. This can be interpreted as a 625% increase in risk of breast cancer, which highlights the magnitude of the risk in a way that 87% did not for the doctor who had misinterpreted these statistics.

A year is nothing.  Five years is the more significant milestone.

"In a meta-analysis of 29 long-term weight loss studies, more than half of the lost weight was regained within two years, and by five years more than 80% of lost weight was regained."

[https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5764193/](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5764193/)

  
"Conde-Knape said rates of weight gain after stopping Wegovy vary depending on the individual, adding that 'some will come back earlier, some will come later.' Novo Nordisk makes both prescription drugs.

She said available data suggests most individuals will recover most of their weight within five years of stopping an obesity drug, and roughly 50% of their weight after two to three years. Some individuals may actually gain more weight after stopping an obesity drug than they initially lost, Conde-Knape added. Studies have similarly shown weight rebound in people who stop taking Ozempic."

[https://www.cnbc.com/2023/03/29/people-taking-obesity-drugs-ozempic-and-wegovy-gain-weight-once-they-stop-medication.html](https://www.cnbc.com/2023/03/29/people-taking-obesity-drugs-ozempic-and-wegovy-gain-weight-once-they-stop-medication.html)

But 80% is not 100%.  Some people are constitutionally capable of keeping the weight off without need of pharmaceutical help.  Since losing weight is easier than maintaining weight loss, those people never needed Wegovy to begin with.

That’s the million dollar question…!  I can tell you that in general I am super healthy, I exercise, eat healthy, cook a lot of dried beans and brown rice and vegetables, eat fruit and whole grains and meats—but not too much—and have been dieting for the last 15 years trying to lose the baby weight!  Those babies are now 26 and 30 years old, both by C-section, that was my only prior overnight hospitalizations, and my only risk factor for bowel obstruction, from possible adhesions (internal scarring).  

I didn’t even have many bad side effects from Ozempic, some occasional very mild constipation that would clear up within 24 hours with stool softeners/more liquids/lower body exercise.  This only happened 2-3 times a month, maybe.  Eating something greasy might bring on diarrhea, I consider that typical.  No sulphur burps, no heartburn, no gas bloating, no vomiting or nausea.

Just very sudden severe abdominal pain and cramping.  Docs thought it might be appendicitis at first.  I was vomiting, couldn’t hold anything down, even liquids.  CT scan confirmed bowel obstruction, I was in ICU that evening and had emergency surgery with 30cm bowel removed—with gangrene!  

I’m a former Medical Assistant and surgery scheduler for general surgeons— I questioned the surgeon and he said he saw adhesions down lower, but not in the area of the obstruction.  The pathology report showed no mass, no cancer.  I did heal up very fast, I spent 9 days in the hospital, with a very ugly vertical scar— the surgeon attempted to do this laparoscopically, but ended up having to do an open surgery, hence the big incision and scar.

So…my gut feeling is that yes, the Ozempic caused it.  I searched online and there are a few cases of bowel obstruction related to Ozempic, but not so many to make a correlation, is my feeling.  There are SO many people who take it without serious issues like this.  Prior C-sections or any abdominal surgery does put a person at higher risk for it.

I’m still glad I took Ozempic to lose this weight.  I think I was solidly prediabetic and insulin resistant, plus menopausal— huge hurdles to losing weight, even when I did WW and went to the gym almost daily, walked, and did yoga classes 3x week, I could only lose about 20lbs.  My triglycerides were sky high even if my cholesterol level was okay…I was just a year or two from becoming a full blown type 2 diabetic.

I’m roughly 50lbs lighter, I haven’t been this slim or healthy since my early 20s.  I am no longer prediabetic, my triglycerides are low (also thanks to statin med), I’m exercising even more now, and I’m more active too.  We moved abroad and no longer own a car, my daily steps automatically tripled walking and taking public transportation.  No more sitting on my butt to drive to Costco and driving back to stuff my freezer full of food I probably shouldn’t eat…

But would I take Ozempic again?  No.

8 months post-operation, I just tried to maintain my weight, give or take +/- 5lbs.  Now I am actively trying to diet again, the old fashioned way, eating right and cutting portions.  Only about 20lbs to get to a “healthy” BMI of 25!
